title: Emerging Areas: Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) and ESG Assurance
description: Comprehensive CA Final Audit MCQs covering Emerging Areas, SDGs, ESG Assurance, and BRSR.

questions.category: SDG and ESG Basics - Definition & Core Concepts
questions.question:
A board-level discussion took place at GreenTerra Ltd., an Indian multi-sector conglomerate, regarding the alignment of their 5-year capital expenditure roadmap with the principles of sustainable development. During the session, the directors evaluated the fundamental premise governing sustainable development as recognized in global reporting and assurance standards. Consider the following statements:

Statement 1: Sustainable development is development that tries to meet the needs of developing countries to achieve a sustainable world.
Statement 2: Sustainable development is characterized by addressing the needs of the present moment without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Statement 3: Sustainable development completely prioritizes immediate economic returns of developing nations over ecological conservation.

Which of the above statements accurately reflect the core definition and concept of sustainable development as outlined in the sustainability frameworks?
questions.explanation: Sustainable development is defined as development that tries to meet the needs of developing countries to achieve a sustainable world, while fundamentally addressing the needs of the present moment without compromising future generations. Statement 1 is correct because sustainable development specifically focuses on enabling developing countries to achieve a sustainable world. Statement 2 is correct as it captures the Brundtland definition of inter-generational equity. Statement 3 is incorrect because sustainable development does not prioritize immediate economic returns over ecological preservation; rather, it balances economic, environmental, and social needs sustainably.

questions.category: SDG and ESG Basics - 17 Sustainable Development Goals
questions.question:
AquaPure Agrochem Ltd. operates a manufacturing facility situated adjacent to an estuarine river basin discharging treated effluents into coastal waters, while also managing extensive captive forestry plantations on inland hill slopes. During an assurance engagement, the sustainability auditor evaluates AquaPure's mapped disclosures against the United Nations 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

The company has classified its water-treatment monitoring and marine biodiversity conservation under 'Life on Land', while classifying its forest conservation, wildlife corridor protection, and reforestation initiatives under 'Clean Water & Sanitization'.

How should the auditor evaluate the mapping of these initiatives against the recognized 17 SDGs?
options: The mapping is appropriate because environmental goals are interrelated and can be reported interchangeably under any ecological SDG heading.
The mapping is incorrect; marine biodiversity conservation falls under 'Life Below Water', while inland forest conservation and reforestation fall under 'Life on Land'.
The mapping is incorrect; both marine and inland forestry initiatives must be grouped exclusively under 'Affordable & Clean Energy'.
The mapping is appropriate provided the company has obtained prior approval from the National Green Tribunal (NGT) for merged reporting.
questions.explanation: Among the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), specific goals exist for distinct biomes: 'Life Below Water' addresses marine and coastal ecosystems, whereas 'Life on Land' addresses terrestrial ecosystems including forests, land degradation, and biodiversity. 'Clean Water & Sanitization' pertains to drinking water supply, sanitation, and freshwater resource management. Therefore, classifying marine biodiversity under 'Life on Land' and forestry under 'Clean Water & Sanitization' is conceptually flawed. The auditor must advise management that marine initiatives belong under 'Life Below Water' and forestry/land initiatives under 'Life on Land'.

questions.category: SDG and ESG Basics - 17 Sustainable Development Goals
questions.question:
An auditor is evaluating the sustainability reporting framework of a listed manufacturing company. The Chief Sustainability Officer presents a list of four corporate themes and claims each is an officially designated UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG):

Theme I: Decent Work & Economic Growth
Theme II: Responsible Consumption & Production
Theme III: Absolute Corporate Profitability & Market Monopoly
Theme IV: Industry Innovation & Infrastructure

Which of the above themes are recognized among the official 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)?
options: Themes I, II, and IV only
Themes II, III, and IV only
Themes I, II, III, and IV
questions.explanation: The 17 Sustainable Development Goals include: No Poverty; Zero Hunger; Good Health & Well Being; Quality Education; Gender Equality; Clean Water & Sanitization; Affordable & Clean Energy; Decent Work & Economic Growth; Industry Innovation & Infrastructure; Reduced Inequalities; Sustainable Cities & Communities; Responsible Consumption & Production; Climate Action; Life Below Water; Life on Land; Peace, Justice & Strong Institutions; and Partnership for the Goals. 'Absolute Corporate Profitability & Market Monopoly' is not an SDG. Hence, only Themes I, II, and IV are recognized SDGs.

questions.category: Three Pillars of ESG - Environmental Pillar
questions.question:
Apex Power & Utilities Ltd. is preparing its ESG disclosure report. The sustainability team has prepared a classification schedule allocating various operational parameters into the three pillars of ESG: Environment (E), Social (S), and Governance (G).

Consider the following operational elements identified by Apex Power:
1. Transitioning thermal turbines to solar-wind hybrid farms (Renewable energy)
2. Measuring and mitigating toxic emissions and industrial effluent waste
3. Addressing groundwater depletion and severe local aquifer water stress
4. Implementing fair wage collective bargaining and occupational health & safety

Which of the above elements are components of the 'Environment (E)' pillar of ESG reporting?
questions.explanation: The Environmental (E) pillar stands for corporate climate policies, energy use, waste, pollution, and natural resource conservation. It encompasses: (i) Natural Resources (e.g., water stress, coal, electricity, water absorbed); (ii) Pollution & Waste (e.g., toxic emissions and waste); and (iii) Environment Opportunity (e.g., renewable energy). Item 4 (fair wage collective bargaining and occupational health & safety) falls under the Social (S) pillar under 'Human Capital', not the Environment pillar. Thus, items 1, 2, and 3 only belong to the Environmental pillar.

questions.category: Three Pillars of ESG - Social Pillar
questions.question:
Zenith Healthcare Ltd. operates private hospitals and pharmaceutical manufacturing units. In its draft ESG report, the management has grouped various sustainability topics into pillar-wise schedules. The audit committee requests the sustainability assurance practitioner to evaluate whether the items under the 'Social (S)' pillar are correctly classified.

The draft Social (S) pillar schedule contains:
(a) Labour management, employee health and workplace safety
(b) Product safety, pharmacovigilance, and drug quality standards
(c) Community access to affordable healthcare clinics
(d) Board diversity, accounting policies, and anti-bribery tax transparency

Which of the above items genuinely belong to the 'Social (S)' pillar of ESG reporting?
questions.explanation: The Social (S) pillar addresses the relationships an entity has and the reputation it fosters with people and institutions, including labour relations, diversity, and inclusion. Its core elements comprise: (i) Human Capital (labour management, health & safety); (ii) Product Liability (product safety & quality); and (iii) Social Opportunity (access to health care). Item (d) pertains to Corporate Governance (accounting, ownership) and Corporate Behaviour (business ethics, tax transparency), which are elements of the Governance (G) pillar. Therefore, only (a), (b), and (c) represent elements of the Social pillar.

questions.category: Three Pillars of ESG - Governance Pillar
questions.question:
During the assurance engagement of Kuber Capital Ltd., the engagement partner reviews the disclosures under the Governance (G) pillar of ESG. The management asserts that the Governance pillar is restricted purely to compliance with Companies Act statutory filings.

Which of the following statements most accurately reflects the scope and elements of the 'Governance (G)' pillar as recognized in ESG reporting?

Statement 1: Governance is the internal system of practices and procedures an entity adopts to govern itself, make investment decisions, comply with law, and meet the needs of all stakeholders.
Statement 2: The Governance pillar includes Corporate Governance elements such as ownership structure and accounting practices.
Statement 3: The Governance pillar includes Corporate Behaviour elements such as business ethics and tax transparency.
Statement 4: Corporate climate policies and toxic waste management are classified under the Corporate Behaviour element of Governance.
questions.explanation: Governance (G) is the internal system of practices and procedures that an entity adopts to govern itself, make investment decisions, comply with the law, and meet the needs of all stakeholders. It encompasses two major sub-elements: (1) Corporate Governance (ownership structure, accounting) and (2) Corporate Behaviour (business ethics, tax transparency). Statement 4 is incorrect because corporate climate policies and toxic waste emissions belong strictly to the Environmental (E) pillar under 'Pollution & Waste' and 'Natural Resources', not Governance.

questions.category: Three Pillars of ESG - Matching Pillars and Elements
questions.question:
Match the ESG Pillars in Column I with their specific constituent elements and examples in Column II:

Column I (ESG Pillar)
A. Environment (E)
B. Social (S) - Human Capital & Product Liability
C. Social (S) - Social Opportunity
D. Governance (G) - Corporate Behaviour

Column II (Constituent Elements / Examples)
1. Labour management, workplace health & safety, and product safety & quality
2. Natural resources water stress, toxic emissions and waste, renewable energy
3. Business ethics and tax transparency
4. Providing marginalized communities access to healthcare

Which of the following represents the correct matching?
questions.explanation: According to the ESG reporting framework: Environment (E) covers natural resources (water stress), pollution & waste (toxic emissions/waste), and environment opportunity (renewable energy), matching with 2. Social (S) - Human Capital & Product Liability covers labour management, health & safety, and product safety & quality, matching with 1. Social (S) - Social Opportunity covers access to healthcare, matching with 4. Governance (G) - Corporate Behaviour covers business ethics and tax transparency, matching with 3. Hence, the correct match is A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3.

questions.category: Three Pillars of ESG - Nature of Reporting
questions.question:
A newly appointed Chief Financial Officer of an engineering listed firm contends that ESG reporting should strictly consist of quantitative metrics (such as metric tonnes of carbon emissions, megalitres of water consumed, and rupees spent on CSR), and that qualitative descriptions of leadership commitment, human rights policies, and ethical codes should be entirely omitted to avoid subjectivity.

How should the sustainability assurance practitioner evaluate the CFO's contention regarding the nature of ESG reporting?
options: The CFO is correct because assurance standards only permit verification of numerically quantifiable data points.

The CFO is incorrect because ESG reporting is all about disclosure of information and data that explain value added in the three areas, and ESG reporting can be both quantitative and qualitative in nature.
The CFO is correct because qualitative information cannot be audited under any Standard on Sustainability Assurance Engagements.
The CFO is incorrect because ESG reporting must be 100% qualitative narrative descriptions, while quantitative metrics belong only to the statutory financial statements.
questions.explanation: ESG reporting is about disclosing information and data that explain the value added across the three areas (Environmental, Social, and Governance). By its intrinsic nature, ESG reporting can be both quantitative and qualitative. While quantitative data (e.g., emission figures, injury rates) provides measurable performance indicators, qualitative information (e.g., governance structures, human rights policies, grievance mechanisms, strategic vision) provides essential context regarding how value is created and protected. Omitting qualitative disclosures would render the ESG report incomplete and non-compliant with standard reporting frameworks.

questions.category: Sustainability Reporting - Meaning & Expected Benefits
questions.question:
Evaluate the following statements regarding the meaning, scope, and objectives of 'Sustainability Reporting':

Statement 1: Sustainability reporting is an organization's practice of reporting publicly on its economic, environmental, and social impacts, and its contributions towards the goal of sustainable development.
Statement 2: Sustainability reporting refers to information that companies provide about their performance to the outside world on an ad-hoc, irregular basis whenever an environmental crisis occurs.
Statement 3: Sustainability reporting refers to structured performance information provided by companies to the outside world on a regular basis.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Sustainability reporting is an organization's practice of reporting publicly on its economic, environmental, and social impacts, and its contributions towards the goal of sustainable development. Furthermore, it refers to information that companies provide about their performance to the outside world on a regular basis in a structured way (not on an ad-hoc or irregular basis during crises). Thus, Statements 1 and 3 are correct, while Statement 2 is incorrect.

questions.category: Sustainability Reporting - Meaning & Expected Benefits
questions.question:
The managing director of Orion Industrial Solutions Ltd. questions the investment required to publish an annual Sustainability Report, arguing that public sustainability reporting merely adds compliance costs without tangible commercial or strategic advantages.

Based on established sustainability reporting principles, which of the following represent recognized expected benefits of sustainability reporting?

(i) Helping stakeholders understand the organization's performance vis-à-vis sustainability.
(ii) Helping entities focus on long-term value creation by addressing ESG issues, enabling investors to make informed investment decisions.
(iii) Improving the company's own business continuity.
(iv) Putting the entity in a better position with its B2B customers as well as enabling it to acquire new customers.
questions.explanation: Sustainability reporting yields multiple strategic and commercial benefits: (1) it helps stakeholders understand organization performance vis-à-vis sustainability; (2) it helps entities focus on long-term value creation by addressing ESG issues, which investors utilize to make investment decisions; (3) it improves the business continuity of the reporting entity; and (4) it puts entities in a better position with their B2B customers and enables them to acquire new customers who demand sustainable supply chains. All four listed points are recognized expected benefits.

questions.category: Global Trends in Sustainability Reporting
questions.question:
Globally, corporations communicate their sustainability performance through established international frameworks. An assurance practitioner is reviewing the sustainability reports of multinational subsidiaries operating in India.

Which of the following frameworks is recognized as the MOST widely used sustainability reporting framework in the world, alongside other prominent initiatives like the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and the International Integrated Reporting Framework (IIRC)?
questions.explanation: Corporations report their sustainability performance globally through: (i) Global Reporting Initiative (GRI), which is recognized as the most widely used framework in the world; (ii) Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP); and (iii) International Integrated Reporting Framework (IIRC). While CDP and IIRC are prominent global frameworks, GRI is specifically recognized as the most widely used sustainability reporting framework globally.

questions.category: Integrated Reporting - 6 Capitals
questions.question:
Nexus Logistics Ltd. is preparing an Integrated Report under the International Integrated Reporting Framework. The finance controller classifies a bank overdraft facility, funds raised through a commercial paper issue, cash flows generated from warehousing operations, and government green project grants under 'Financial Capital'.

Is this classification consistent with the definition of Financial Capital under Integrated Reporting?
options: Yes, because Financial Capital is the pool of funds that is available to an organization for use in the production of goods or provision of services, obtained through financing (such as debt, equity, or grants) or generated through operations or investments.
No, because Financial Capital is strictly restricted to permanent equity share capital, and debt or operational cash flows must be classified under Manufactured Capital.
No, because government grants must be classified under Social Capital as community assistance.
Yes, provided the pool of funds is invested exclusively in zero-carbon physical assets.
questions.explanation: Under the Integrated Reporting Framework, Financial Capital is defined as the pool of funds that is available to an organization for use in the production of goods or provision of services. It is obtained through financing, such as debt, equity, or grants, or generated through operations or investments. Nexus Logistics Ltd.'s classification of debt, equity, grants, and operational cash flows under Financial Capital is completely aligned with this definition.

questions.category: Integrated Reporting - 6 Capitals
questions.question:
A steel manufacturing enterprise, Vulcan Alloys Ltd., discloses the following resources in its Integrated Report:

Resource X: Specialized blast furnace machinery, automated rolling mill plants, transport railway sidings, and office factory premises.
Resource Y: Iron ore deposits, river water extracted for cooling, coal reserves, and surrounding catchment area biodiversity.

How should Resource X and Resource Y be correctly categorized under the 6 Capitals of Integrated Reporting?
options: Resource X is Manufactured Capital; Resource Y is Natural Capital.
Resource X is Natural Capital; Resource Y is Manufactured Capital.
Both Resource X and Resource Y are Manufactured Capital.
Resource X is Financial Capital; Resource Y is Social Capital.
questions.explanation: In Integrated Reporting, 'Manufactured Capital' consists of human-created, production-oriented equipment and tools available to an organization for use in the production of goods or provision of services, including buildings, equipment, and infrastructure (Resource X). 'Natural Capital' includes all renewable and non-renewable environmental resources and processes that provide goods or services that support past, current, or future prosperity, acting as an input to production (water, land, minerals, forests, ecosystem health) and impacted by organization activities (Resource Y).

questions.category: Integrated Reporting - 6 Capitals
questions.question:
During the audit of an integrated report of a software development firm, the auditor analyzes the company's disclosure under 'Human Capital'. Which of the following elements are genuine components of 'Human Capital' as defined under the 6 Capitals of Integrated Reporting?

1. People's skills, experience, and capacity.
2. Employees' alignment with the organization's governance framework and ethical values.
3. Employees' ability to understand and implement the organization's strategy.
4. Loyalties and motivations for improving processes and their ability to lead.
5. Intellectual property rights, patents, and software source code copyrighted by the company.
questions.explanation: Under the 6 Capitals of Integrated Reporting, Human Capital encompasses people's competencies, capabilities, skills, and experience, including their alignment with the organization's governance framework and ethical values, their ability to understand and implement the organization's strategy, and their loyalties and motivations for improving processes and their ability to lead (Items 1, 2, 3, and 4). In contrast, patents, copyrights, software source code, and R&D-driven innovation belong to 'Intellectual Capital'. Hence, only 1, 2, 3, and 4 constitute Human Capital.

questions.category: Integrated Reporting - 6 Capitals
questions.question:
Consider the following two corporate resources disclosed by an advanced biotech corporation:

Capital P: Key stakeholder relationships, mutual trust, common values and shared behaviour established within local communities, along with the company's social license to operate.
Capital Q: R&D investments leading to patented genetic sequencing technologies, proprietary software algorithms, and institutionalized innovation systems that drive future earning potential.

Which of the following correctly pairs Capital P and Capital Q with their recognized designations under the 6 Capitals of Integrated Reporting?
options: Capital P is Social Capital; Capital Q is Intellectual Capital.
Capital P is Human Capital; Capital Q is Financial Capital.
Capital P is Intellectual Capital; Capital Q is Social Capital.
Capital P is Natural Capital; Capital Q is Manufactured Capital.
questions.explanation: Social Capital encompasses the institutions and relationships established within each community, stakeholders, and other networks to enhance individual and collective well-being, including common values, shared behaviour, key relationships, trust, loyalty, and the organization's social license to operate (Capital P). Intellectual Capital is a key element in an organization's future earning potential, reflecting a tight link between investments in R&D, innovation, and human resources, comprising organizational knowledge and intangibles (Capital Q).

questions.category: Integrated Reporting - Regulatory Applicability
questions.question:
Pinnacle Consumer Goods Ltd. is ranked 350th among listed entities on the National Stock Exchange based on market capitalization as of 31st March 2024. During a board meeting, a director states that the company is legally mandated under SEBI regulations to publish an Integrated Report under the IIRC framework for the financial year, and failure to do so will attract statutory penalties.

Evaluate the director's statement in light of the regulatory framework governing Integrated Reporting in India:
options: The director's statement is incorrect because Integrated Reporting is voluntary for the top 500 listed entities.
The director's statement is correct because Integrated Reporting is mandatory for all top 500 listed entities.
The director's statement is incorrect because Integrated Reporting is mandatory only for the top 100 listed entities.
The director's statement is correct because any company falling in the top 1000 listed entities must mandatorily publish an Integrated Report instead of BRSR.
questions.explanation: In India, while SEBI has mandated Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) for the top 1,000 listed entities, Integrated Reporting (under the IIRC framework) was introduced on a voluntary basis for the top 500 listed entities. Therefore, the director's claim that Integrated Reporting is legally mandatory and subject to penalties is incorrect; it is voluntary for top 500 listed companies.

questions.category: BRSR - Applicability and Structure
questions.question:
Titanium Engineering Ltd. is an Indian public company listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). As of March 31, 2024, its market capitalization ranks 850th among all listed companies in India. The CFO claims that because the company is outside the top 500 listed companies, it is completely exempt from submitting a Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR).

Is the CFO's claim correct?
options: No; top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalization are required to mandatorily furnish BRSR.
Yes; BRSR is mandatory only for the top 100 listed entities, while top 500 entities have voluntary compliance.
Yes; companies ranked between 501 and 1,000 are only required to submit voluntary Integrated Reports.
No; BRSR is mandatory for every unlisted and listed company in India regardless of market capitalization.
questions.explanation: Under SEBI regulations, the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalization are required to mandatorily furnish the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR). Since Titanium Engineering Ltd. is ranked 850th by market capitalization, it falls squarely within the top 1,000 listed companies and must mandatorily prepare and furnish the BRSR. The CFO's claim is incorrect.

questions.category: BRSR - Applicability and Structure
questions.question:
The BRSR reporting questionnaire prescribed by SEBI is structured into three distinct sections. Match the sections in Column I with their respective contents in Column II:

Column I (BRSR Section)
A. Section A: General Disclosures
B. Section B: Management and Process Disclosures
C. Section C: Principle-wise Performance Disclosures

Column II (Mandated Contents)
1. Contains details related to leadership, governance, and management processes.
2. Contains details of the company regarding its products, services, employees, and its subsidiary/associate companies, etc.
3. Contains Essential indicators (mandatory disclosures regarding core elements) and Leadership indicators (optional disclosures regarding additional inputs, programmes, life cycle assessments, etc.).

Which of the following represents the correct matching?
questions.explanation: The BRSR reporting questionnaire is divided into three sections: Section A: General Disclosures contains details of the company regarding its products, services, employees, and subsidiary/associate companies (matching 2); Section B: Management and Process Disclosures contains details related to leadership, governance, and management processes (matching 1); and Section C: Principle-wise Performance Disclosures covers Essential Indicators (mandatory disclosures on core elements) and Leadership Indicators (optional disclosures on additional inputs, life cycle assessments, etc., matching 3). The correct match is A-2, B-1, C-3.

questions.category: BRSR - Section C Disclosures
questions.question:
An ESG assurance team is conducting an initial review of Section C (Principle-wise Performance Disclosures) of a client's BRSR. The client omitted several 'Essential Indicators' arguing that they are non-binding recommendations, but disclosed select 'Leadership Indicators' to showcase positive corporate branding.

How should the assurance practitioner evaluate this disclosure approach under BRSR Section C?
options: The client's approach is acceptable because companies have discretion to choose either Essential or Leadership indicators under Section C.

The client's approach is non-compliant; Essential indicators represent mandatory disclosures regarding core elements that must be furnished, whereas Leadership indicators are optional disclosures covering additional programmes, inputs, and life cycle assessments.
The client's approach is compliant provided the omitted Essential indicators are compensated by double the number of Leadership indicators.
The client's approach is non-compliant because both Essential indicators and Leadership indicators are strictly mandatory for all top 1000 listed entities.
questions.explanation: Section C of the BRSR is divided into two tiers of performance disclosures: (1) Essential indicators, which are mandatory disclosures that include data regarding core elements of each principle; and (2) Leadership indicators, which are optional disclosures that include additional inputs, advanced sustainability programmes, life-cycle assessments, etc. An entity cannot omit mandatory Essential indicators while selectively disclosing optional Leadership indicators. The practitioner must qualify or report this non-compliance.

questions.category: Principles of BRSR - ESG Pillar Categorization
questions.question: The Nine Principles of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) are mapped across the three components of ESG (Environment, Social, and Governance). What is the exact mathematical and conceptual distribution of the nine BRSR principles across these three pillars?
options: 2 in Environment, 3 in Social, and 4 in Governance
3 in Environment, 3 in Social, and 3 in Governance
1 in Environment, 4 in Social, and 4 in Governance
4 in Environment, 2 in Social, and 3 in Governance
questions.explanation: The nine principles in BRSR are categorized into the ESG components of Environment, Social, and Governance with: two principles in Environment (Principles 2 and 6), three principles in Social (Principles 3, 4, and 5), and four principles in Governance (Principles 1, 7, 8, and 9). This reflects exactly 2 in Environment, 3 in Social, and 4 in Governance.

questions.category: BRSR Principle 1 - Ethics, Transparency and Accountability
questions.question:
Alpha Chemical Ltd., a top-500 listed manufacturer, discovered an accidental discharge of hazardous solvent into a municipal storm drain. The management resolved to internally remediate the site but decided not to disclose the incident in its BRSR disclosures to avoid panic among institutional shareholders. Furthermore, Alpha's management refused to engage with a key raw-material supplier that had repeatedly violated basic ethical anti-bribery standards, claiming Alpha's internal code does not apply outside its corporate perimeter.

Evaluating this scenario under Principle 1 of BRSR (Ethics, Transparency and Accountability), which of the following statements are correct?

Statement 1: Entities should develop policies and procedures for work areas so that ethics is not compromised, and information relating to policies and procedures should be made available to stakeholders.
Statement 2: In case of adverse effects or incidents, more care has to be taken for transparent disclosures rather than suppressing information.
Statement 3: Entities in the value chain should be encouraged to adopt BRSR principles, and entities should proactively respond to outside entities (such as suppliers) that violate BRSR principles.
Statement 4: Principle 1 permits management to suppress adverse environmental effects if revealing them harms share price.
questions.explanation: Under BRSR Principle 1 (Businesses should conduct and govern themselves with integrity, and in a manner that is Ethical, Transparent and Accountable), the essence of core elements requires: (i) developing policies and procedures for work areas so ethics is not compromised; (ii) making information relating to policies/procedures available to stakeholders; (iii) taking greater care for transparent disclosures in case of adverse effects; (iv) encouraging value chain entities to adopt these principles; and (v) proactively responding to outside entities (suppliers, etc.) that violate BRSR principles. Statement 4 is completely contrary to Principle 1. Hence, Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct.

questions.category: BRSR Principle 2 - Safe and Sustainable Goods and Services
questions.question:
EcoConsumer Products Ltd. manufactures household cleaning appliances. The R&D division has developed energy-efficient and recyclable appliances. However, the sales and marketing division refuses to provide user manuals explaining customer consumer rights, safe handling instructions, or recycling options, arguing that customer education is not a producer responsibility. Furthermore, production processes rely heavily on virgin rare-earth minerals without exploring reuse or recycling technologies.

Evaluating this situation under BRSR Principle 2 (Safe and Sustainable Goods and Services), what are the core responsibilities of the entity?

(i) Making sure that goods, services, and operations result in a better life for consumers.
(ii) Educating consumers and clients about their rights.
(iii) Devising production methods and technologies (R&D) to make products sustainable.
(iv) Reducing over-exploitation of natural resources through reuse and recycling of resources.
questions.explanation: Under BRSR Principle 2 (Businesses should provide goods and services in a manner that is sustainable and safe), entities should ensure that their goods, services, and operations result in a better life for consumers. The core elements mandate that: (1) entities are responsible for educating their consumers and clients about their rights; (2) production methods and technologies (R&D) must be devised to make products sustainable; and (3) entities should reduce over-exploitation of natural resources by reuse and recycling of resources. All four statements reflect core elements of Principle 2.

questions.category: BRSR Principle 3 - Employee Well-being
questions.question:
A textile garment manufacturing firm employs 2,500 permanent workers and 3,000 contract workers in its supply chain factories. An assurance review reveals the following practices:
- Factory managers retain juvenile workers under the age of 14 during peak seasonal demand.
- Contract workers are paid wages below the statutory living wage and experience delays of 60 to 90 days in wage disbursement.
- Mandatory 16-hour shifts are enforced seven days a week, with no mechanism for work-life balance.
- No safety equipment or harassment prevention policies exist for female shop-floor workers.

Under BRSR Principle 3 (Promote well-being of all employees including those in the value chain), which of the following represent non-negotiable core requirements?

1. Preventing all kinds of child labour, bonded labour, and any other involuntary labour.
2. Ensuring timely payment of wages as per living wages and respecting employee dignity.
3. Establishing a system in which the work-life balance of employees is not compromised.
4. Creation of a workplace that is safe and free of harassment.
5. Skill development and training of the workforce.
6. Ensuring compliance with all regulatory requirements regarding employees.
questions.explanation: BRSR Principle 3 mandates the promotion of the well-being of all employees, including those in the value chain. Its core elements require: ensuring compliance with all regulatory requirements regarding employees; preventing all kinds of child labour, bonded labour, and involuntary labour; maintaining a system where work-life balance is not compromised; ensuring timely payment of wages as per living wages and respecting worker dignity; providing skill development and training; and creating a workplace that is safe and free of harassment. All six listed points represent mandatory core elements of Principle 3.

questions.category: BRSR Principle 4 - Stakeholders Interests & Responsiveness
questions.question:
HeavyMetals Mining Ltd. planned an open-cast mining project in a forested tribal belt. The company obtained environmental clearance but kept local indigenous communities completely uninformed about the impending displacement, groundwater depletion, and air pollution risks. When community representatives protested, the board asserted that private corporations owe disclosure duties exclusively to equity shareholders and have no obligation to communicate operational impacts to non-investor stakeholders.

How does this corporate stance hold up against BRSR Principle 4 (Respect for Stakeholders' Interests and Responsiveness)?
options: It is fully compliant because Indian corporate law recognizes shareholders as the sole legitimate stakeholders of a listed company.

It is non-compliant because entities must be transparent and communicate with stakeholders about the impacts of their operations and business decisions on people and nature, and fairly share benefits in an equitable manner.
It is compliant provided the company deposits 2% of net profits in a designated CSR bank account.
It is non-compliant solely if the protesting community holds at least 10% of the company's voting shares.
questions.explanation: Principle 4 of BRSR states that businesses should respect the interests of and be responsive to all stakeholders. The core elements highlight that: (1) entities have to be transparent and communicate with stakeholders about the impacts of their operations and business decisions on people and nature; and (2) entities should fairly share benefits to stakeholders in an equitable manner. Limiting communication and responsiveness only to financial shareholders violates the foundational essence of Principle 4.

questions.category: BRSR Principle 5 - Respect and Promote Human Rights
questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding BRSR Principle 5 (Respect and Promote Human Rights):

Statement 1: Principle 5 refers to human rights issues that happen directly or indirectly due to the operations of a business.
Statement 2: Entities should have a clear understanding of human rights from the perspective of the Constitution of India.
Statement 3: Entities should integrate human rights elements into their policies and procedures and recognize and respect the human rights of all relevant stakeholders.
Statement 4: Under Principle 5, a corporate entity is only responsible for direct human rights violations occurring on its own owned premises, and bears zero responsibility for human rights abuses caused indirectly by its supply chain or operations.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Under BRSR Principle 5 (Businesses should respect and promote human rights), the core elements emphasize: (i) addressing human rights issues that occur directly or indirectly due to business operations; (ii) having a clear understanding of human rights from the perspective of the Indian Constitution; (iii) integrating human rights elements into policies and procedures; and (iv) recognizing and respecting the human rights of all relevant stakeholders. Statement 4 is incorrect because Principle 5 expressly covers both direct and indirect human rights impacts arising from business operations.

questions.category: BRSR Principle 6 - Protection & Restoration of Environment
questions.question:
A chemical manufacturing company, ChemTech Ltd., is formulating its environmental management strategy. The board discusses the requirements under BRSR Principle 6 (Protection and Restoration of Environment).

Which of the following actions align directly with the essence of core elements associated with Principle 6?

1. Making use of natural and manmade resources in an optimum manner.
2. Having policies and procedures in place to assess and rectify environmental impacts.
3. Measuring organizational performance relating to prevention of pollution, energy use, and resource consumption.
4. Contributing towards climate change resilience in line with national action plans.
5. Comparing company activities with industry benchmarks to reduce, reuse, and recycle resources.
questions.explanation: Under BRSR Principle 6 (Businesses should respect, protect, and make efforts to restore the environment), the essence of core elements includes: (1) optimum use of natural and manmade resources; (2) establishing policies and procedures to assess and rectify environmental impact; (3) measuring performance relating to pollution prevention, energy use, etc.; (4) contributing towards climate change resilience in line with national action plans; and (5) benchmarking activities against industry standards to reduce, reuse, and recycle resources. All five items are core elements of Principle 6.

questions.category: BRSR Principle 7 - Public & Regulatory Policy Influence
questions.question:
An industry trade association representing major pharmaceutical manufacturers engages in lobbying activities with the central government regarding price controls and environmental emission limits. One member firm secretly advocates for policies that would grant exemptions to existing large players while creating prohibitive licensing barriers for new startups, thereby stifling market competition.

Evaluating this conduct under BRSR Principle 7 (Influence on Public and Regulatory Policy), which of the following statements represents the correct principle governing policy formulation?

Statement 1: Businesses operate within the statutory and legislative policy framework of governing authorities, and their policy advocacy must meet core elements holistically.
Statement 2: Collective associations (such as trade groups and industry chambers) should be utilized while undertaking policy formulation.
Statement 3: Policy formulation advocacy by organizations should actively encourage fair competition and prevent human rights abuse.
questions.explanation: Principle 7 of BRSR recognizes that businesses operate within the framework of statutory and legislative policies of governing authorities. It specifically mandates that: (i) core elements should be met holistically when organizations undertake policy advocacy/formulation; (ii) collective associations, trade groups, and industry chambers should be utilized in policy advocacy; and (iii) policy formulation advocacy must encourage fair competition and prevent human rights abuses. Stifling competition violates Principle 7. All three statements are correct.

questions.category: BRSR Principle 8 - Inclusive Growth & Equitable Development
questions.question:
InfraMega Power Corp. acquired 1,200 acres of rural agricultural land for an ultra-mega thermal power plant. Over 400 rural families were forcibly evicted without notice, and no resettlement or compensation was offered. The company claimed that because its general CSR wing spends funds on urban computer literacy centers, it has fulfilled its inclusive development obligations.

Evaluate this situation against the essence of core elements under BRSR Principle 8 (Promote Inclusive Growth and Equitable Development):

(i) Entities must have systems in place to identify and address impacts of their activities on people, review adverse impacts, and make mitigation action plans.
(ii) Entities should bring up creative products and technologies that help marginalized communities and review CSR priorities to help marginalized groups.
(iii) Entities should ensure that displacement or relocation of communities does not happen; otherwise, they must provide fair compensation to affected people.
(iv) Entities can lawfully displace communities without compensation if they spend at least 2% of their net profits on unrelated CSR initiatives.
questions.explanation: BRSR Principle 8 emphasizes close participation and collaboration for better livelihood and assistance to marginalized communities. Its core elements mandate that entities should: identify and address impacts on people; review adverse impacts and make mitigation plans; create products/technologies helping marginalized groups; align CSR priorities towards marginalized communities; and critically, ensure displacement/relocation does not occur, or otherwise provide fair compensation to affected people. Spending money on unrelated CSR does not excuse uncompensated forced displacement. Thus, (i), (ii), and (iii) are correct, and (iv) is incorrect.

questions.category: BRSR Principle 9 - Value to Consumers Responsibly
questions.question:
TeleMax Digital Ltd., a telecom and smartphone manufacturing company, engaged in the following marketing practices:
1. It embedded untraceable background spyware in consumer devices that secretly harvested and sold user personal data without consent.
2. Its marketing advertisements concealed substantial hidden daily network access charges.
3. It locked devices so users could not switch to competitor network providers, thereby restricting freedom of choice.
4. It shut down its customer grievance redressal portal, leaving consumer complaints unanswered.

Evaluating these practices under BRSR Principle 9 (Provide Value to Consumers in a Responsible Manner), which core elements of Principle 9 have been violated by TeleMax Digital Ltd.?

(a) Maintaining customer right to privacy when handling consumer data.
(b) Ensuring misleading information is not given to customers while advertising.
(c) Not preventing freedom of choice while designing and marketing products.
(d) Making available a transparent grievance redressal and feedback system for customers.
(e) Informing customers on safe ways of using and disposal of products and disclosing adverse impacts.
questions.explanation: The core purpose of business under Principle 9 is to provide useful products and services to customers for reasonable profits. The core elements mandate: transparently disclosing adverse impacts; reducing negative impacts of products; educating on safe usage and disposal; ensuring misleading information is not given during advertising; maintaining customer right to privacy when handling data; not restricting freedom of choice during product design and marketing; and providing a transparent grievance redressal and feedback system. TeleMax has violated every single one of these foundational requirements.

questions.category: Principles of BRSR - Comprehensive Matching
questions.question:
Match the BRSR Principles in Column I with their primary thematic focus in Column II:

Column I (Principle)
A. Principle 1
B. Principle 3
C. Principle 6
D. Principle 9

Column II (Thematic Focus)
1. Protection and restoration of environment, pollution prevention, and resource recycling
2. Ethics, transparency, accountability, and proactive value-chain integrity
3. Value to consumers, customer data privacy, freedom of choice, and grievance redressal
4. Well-being of all employees including value chain, living wages, work-life balance, and safety

Which of the following represents the correct matching?
questions.explanation: Principle 1 deals with Ethics, Transparency, and Accountability (matching 2). Principle 3 deals with Promoting the well-being of all employees including those in the value chain (matching 4). Principle 6 deals with Protection and Restoration of Environment (matching 1). Principle 9 deals with Providing Value to Consumers in a Responsible Manner (matching 3). Hence, the correct matching combination is A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3.

questions.category: Assurance in BRSR - Standards & ICAI Pronouncement
questions.question: With the increasing importance of sustainability disclosures in India, ICAI has issued professional assurance pronouncements to govern sustainability audits. Which specific Standard has been recently issued by ICAI to deal with all assurance engagements on an entity's sustainability information?
options: Guidance Note on Tax Audit under Section 44AB only
Accounting Standard (AS) 18 on Related Party Disclosures
questions.explanation: To provide authoritative guidance and establish rigorous assurance criteria, the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) has issued the Standard on Sustainability Assurance Engagements (SSAE). This Standard deals with all assurance engagements on an entity's sustainability information, establishing professional requirements for practitioners conducting sustainability verifications.

questions.category: Methodology to Provide Assurance on BRSR - Procedural Sequence
questions.question:
An ESG assurance audit firm is formalizing its standard operating procedure (SOP) for conducting assurance on BRSR reports of listed corporate clients. Arrange the following verification phases into the correct chronological sequence as recognized in the methodology to provide assurance on BRSR:

Step 1: On-site assessment/verification of ESG report
Step 2: Submission of findings of on-site assessment and document review
Step 3: Preliminary review of ESG report
Step 4: Review of responses and clarifications on findings
Step 5: Preparation of assessment/verification report including final results of assessment
Step 6: Issuance of assessment report and assessment statement

Which of the following represents the correct sequential order?
options: Step 3 -> Step 1 -> Step 2 -> Step 4 -> Step 5 -> Step 6
Step 1 -> Step 3 -> Step 2 -> Step 5 -> Step 4 -> Step 6
Step 3 -> Step 2 -> Step 1 -> Step 4 -> Step 6 -> Step 5
Step 6 -> Step 5 -> Step 4 -> Step 3 -> Step 2 -> Step 1
questions.explanation: The established methodology to provide assurance on BRSR follows a structured logical sequence: (1) Preliminary review of ESG report; (2) On-site assessment/verification of ESG report; (3) Submission of findings of on-site assessment and document review; (4) Review of responses and clarifications on findings from management; (5) Preparation of assessment/verification report including final results of assessment; and (6) Issuance of assessment report and assessment statement. Therefore, the correct chronological order is 3 -> 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6.

questions.category: Methodology to Provide Assurance on BRSR - Procedural Sequence
questions.question: During the assurance engagement of GreenGrid Power Ltd.'s BRSR, the assurance team completed its document review and physical inspection of emissions control units at three generating stations. The team identified several discrepancies between logbook meter readings and disclosed GHG numbers. What is the immediate next step the assurance team must undertake before preparing the final assessment report?
options: Immediately issue a publicly adverse assessment statement without discussing findings with management.
Submit the findings of on-site assessment and document review to management, and review management's responses and clarifications on those findings.
Revoke the client's environmental clearance license with the Pollution Control Board.
File a criminal complaint with the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO).
questions.explanation: In accordance with the BRSR assurance methodology, after completing the preliminary review and on-site assessment/verification, the practitioner submits the findings of the on-site assessment and document review to entity management. The practitioner then reviews the responses and clarifications provided by management on those findings before proceeding to prepare the final assessment/verification report and issuing the final assessment statement.

questions.category: Role of Auditor - Climate-Related Risks in Audit of FS
questions.question:
CA. Rakesh is the statutory auditor of PetroCarbon Refineries Ltd. for FY 2023-24. During audit planning, Rakesh asserts: 'As a statutory auditor under the Companies Act, 2013, my sole responsibility is verifying debits, credits, and vouchers. Climate-related risks, carbon taxation liabilities, asset decommissioning obligations, and environmental regulations belong exclusively to ESG consultants and have zero relevance to the audit of financial statements.'

Evaluate CA. Rakesh's assertion in light of auditing pronouncements:
options: CA. Rakesh is correct because financial statement audits are completely insulated from environmental and climate factors.

CA. Rakesh is incorrect because in developing an understanding of the entity, the auditor should consider climate-related risks and how these risks may be relevant to the audit of financial statements, obtaining reasonable assurance that financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement.
CA. Rakesh is correct provided the company has not received a formal penalty notice from the Ministry of Environment.
CA. Rakesh is incorrect because the statutory auditor is personally responsible for eliminating all carbon emissions of the audit client.
questions.explanation: The role of the statutory auditor is to obtain reasonable assurance whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement due to fraud or error. In developing an understanding of the entity and its environment, the auditor should actively consider climate-related risks and how these risks may be relevant to the audit (such as asset impairment, useful life of polluting plant, provisions for environmental rehabilitation, going concern). Dismissing climate risks as completely irrelevant is a failure of audit planning.

questions.category: Role of Auditor - Climate-Related Risks in Audit of FS
questions.question:
CoalThermal Energy Ltd. operates obsolete coal-fired power plants facing mandatory phase-out under national net-zero legislation within 3 years. This legislative mandate severely impacts asset valuations, depreciation schedules, and decommissioning provisions. Management did not disclose these climate impacts in the notes to the financial statements, but included glowing qualitative remarks in the Directors' Report. The statutory auditor plans to issue an unmodified opinion without mentioning anything in the audit report.

What is the statutory auditor's duty regarding climate-related disclosures in the financial statements?
options: The auditor has no duty regarding climate disclosures as long as the balance sheet figures balance mathematically.

The auditor should determine whether the entity has appropriately disclosed relevant climate-related information in the financial statements as per the applicable Financial Reporting Framework (FRF) before considering climate-related matters in the auditor's report.
The auditor should verify disclosures only if the company voluntarily adopts integrated reporting.
The auditor is legally required to draft the missing notes on climate change and insert them directly into the published annual accounts.
questions.explanation: The auditor must determine whether the entity has appropriately disclosed relevant climate-related information in the financial statements in accordance with the applicable Financial Reporting Framework (FRF) before considering climate-related matters in the auditor's report. If material climate-related risks, asset write-downs, or contingent liabilities are omitted from the financial statement disclosures, the financial statements do not achieve fair presentation under the FRF, requiring an appropriate modification or communication in the audit report.

questions.category: Role of Auditor - Climate-Related Risks in Audit of FS
questions.question:
Solaria Infrastructure Ltd. has appropriately and extensively disclosed in Note 34 to its financial statements the catastrophic financial exposure arising from a newly enacted climate regulation that bans groundwater extraction for thermal cooling, threatening plant operations. The matter is appropriately accounted for and transparently disclosed, and the auditor agrees with the accounting treatment and disclosures. However, given intense stakeholder pressure for transparency regarding climate risks, the engagement partner ponders the communication mechanism in the auditor's report.

Which of the following reporting actions is most appropriate under auditing principles?
options: The auditor must issue an adverse audit opinion because climate change poses an inherent threat to humanity.

The auditor's report is a key mechanism of communication to users; in such circumstances, it may warrant inclusion of an Emphasis of Matter (EOM) paragraph to draw attention to disclosures that are of fundamental importance to users' understanding of the financial statements.
The auditor is strictly prohibited from mentioning climate matters in the auditor's report under any circumstances.
The auditor must resign immediately to avoid association with climate-sensitive industries.
questions.explanation: The auditor's report is a key mechanism of communication to users about the audit performed, detailing the opinion and auditor's responsibilities. In circumstances where climate-related risks or events are appropriately disclosed in the financial statements but are of fundamental importance to users' understanding of the financial statements, it may warrant the inclusion of an Emphasis of Matter (EOM) paragraph (referencing the specific disclosure note) to draw users' attention to those fundamental matters.

questions.category: Role of Auditor - Climate-Related Risks in Audit of FS
questions.question:
In the annual report of EcoCement Ltd., the statutory financial statements record a provision of Rs. 15 Crores for environmental carbon tax penalties, and disclose that two clinker kilns were shut down due to non-compliance with emission standards. However, in the 'Chairman's Statement' and the BRSR included in the same Annual Report, the company proclaims: 'Our operations achieved 100% zero-pollution compliance with zero regulatory penalties or plant shutdowns across all manufacturing sites.'

What is the statutory auditor's professional responsibility regarding this contradiction?
options: The auditor has zero responsibility because the Chairman's Statement and BRSR fall outside the audited financial statements.

Under SA 720, the auditor should read other information for consistency with information disclosed in the financial statements and information publicly communicated to stakeholders outside the financial statements, and take appropriate action if a material inconsistency is identified.
The auditor must amend the audited financial statements to match the optimistic statements in the Chairman's speech.
The auditor should ignore the inconsistency since BRSR is governed by SEBI while financial statements are governed by MCA.
questions.explanation: Under SA 720 (The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Other Information), the auditor is required to read the other information (which includes the Chairman's Statement, Directors' Report, and BRSR in the annual report) to identify material inconsistencies between the other information and the financial statements, as well as the auditor's knowledge obtained during the audit. The auditor must consider consistency with disclosures in the financial statements and publicly communicated stakeholder information, and pursue appropriate corrective actions if inconsistencies exist.

questions.category: Standard on Sustainability Assurance Engagements (SSAE) 3000
questions.question:
The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) recently issued SSAE 3000 (Assurance Engagements on Sustainability Information). Which of the following statements most accurately describes the nature and operational scope of SSAE 3000?

Statement 1: SSAE 3000 deals with assurance engagements on an entity's sustainability information.
Statement 2: SSAE 3000 is an umbrella standard applicable to all assurance engagements on sustainability information.
Statement 3: SSAE 3000 applies exclusively to audits of historical financial statements of listed power distribution companies.
Statement 4: SSAE 3000 replaces the Companies Act, 2013 for all statutory financial audits.
questions.explanation: ICAI issued SSAE 3000 - Assurance Engagements on Sustainability Information. This Standard deals with assurance engagements on an entity's sustainability information and serves as an umbrella standard applicable to all assurance engagements on sustainability information across diverse topics (GHG emissions, BRSR, water footprints, social metrics). Statements 3 and 4 are incorrect because SSAE 3000 does not apply to statutory financial audits under the Companies Act, nor does it replace the statute.

questions.category: Standard on Sustainability Assurance Engagements (SSAE) 3000
questions.question:
SSAE 3000 outlines the framework and responsibilities for conducting assurance engagements on sustainability disclosures. According to SSAE 3000, who are the intended users of this Standard?

(i) Assurance providers providing assurance on sustainability information.
(ii) Entities seeking to engage a professional auditor for sustainability assurance.
(iii) Regulators, investors, and other users of sustainability reporting data.
questions.explanation: SSAE 3000 explicitly identifies three key categories of intended users: (1) Assurance providers who provide assurance on sustainability information; (2) Entities seeking to engage a professional auditor to perform sustainability assurance; and (3) Regulators, investors, and other users who rely on verified sustainability reporting data. Therefore, all three groups are intended users of SSAE 3000.

questions.category: Integrated Scenario - BRSR Principles & ESG Assurance
questions.question:
CASE STUDY:
GreenHorizon Infrastructure Ltd., a top-500 listed infrastructure company, undertook the construction of a 200 km greenfield highway corridor. During the financial year 2023-24, the following issues arose:
1. The project displaced 600 tribal families from forest land. The company refused to pay rehabilitation compensation, claiming its 2% statutory CSR expenditure on urban digital schools exempts it from local resettlement obligations.
2. In its draft BRSR report, the company reported 100% compliance with human rights and zero employee grievances, despite 45 pending sexual harassment and bonded labour complaints before the Internal Complaints Committee (ICC).
3. The company disclosed that it adopted renewable solar power for highway toll plazas, which it classified under 'Governance (G) - Corporate Governance'.
4. The management approached CA. Ananya to issue an assurance report on its BRSR under SSAE 3000, requesting her to bypass on-site site visits and skip reviewing management responses to avoid delays.

With reference to Issue 1 (tribal displacement and CSR reallocation), how should CA. Ananya evaluate the company's position under BRSR Principle 8 (Promote Inclusive Growth and Equitable Development)?
options: The company's position is fully compliant because CSR spending under Section 135 overrides BRSR operational principles.

The company's position violates Principle 8; entities must ensure displacement or relocation of communities does not happen, or otherwise provide fair compensation to affected people, and CSR priorities cannot be used as an excuse to avoid mitigating adverse impacts on displaced communities.
The company is exempt from paying displacement compensation if the highway project is declared a public utility project.
The company's position is compliant provided the affected families are given free toll passes on the newly constructed highway.
questions.explanation: Under BRSR Principle 8, entities must have systems in place to identify and address impacts of their activities on people, review adverse impacts, and make mitigation action plans. Critically, entities must ensure that displacement or relocation of communities does not happen, or otherwise provide fair compensation to affected people. Spending money on unrelated urban CSR activities does not absolve the company of its fundamental duty under Principle 8 to compensate and rehabilitate displaced tribal families.

questions.category: Integrated Scenario - BRSR Principles & ESG Assurance
questions.question:
CASE STUDY:
GreenHorizon Infrastructure Ltd., a top-500 listed infrastructure company, undertook the construction of a 200 km greenfield highway corridor. During the financial year 2023-24, the following issues arose:
1. The project displaced 600 tribal families from forest land. The company refused to pay rehabilitation compensation, claiming its 2% statutory CSR expenditure on urban digital schools exempts it from local resettlement obligations.
2. In its draft BRSR report, the company reported 100% compliance with human rights and zero employee grievances, despite 45 pending sexual harassment and bonded labour complaints before the Internal Complaints Committee (ICC).
3. The company disclosed that it adopted renewable solar power for highway toll plazas, which it classified under 'Governance (G) - Corporate Governance'.
4. The management approached CA. Ananya to issue an assurance report on its BRSR under SSAE 3000, requesting her to bypass on-site site visits and skip reviewing management responses to avoid delays.

With reference to Issue 2 (suppression of 45 pending harassment and bonded labour complaints in the draft BRSR), which BRSR principles have been directly breached by the company?
options: Principle 1 (Ethics, Transparency and Accountability) and Principle 3 (Promote well-being of all employees including those in the value chain)
No principle is breached because pending complaints are not final adjudications and need not be disclosed in BRSR.
questions.explanation: Suppressing 45 pending complaints relating to sexual harassment and bonded labour breaches both Principle 1 and Principle 3. Under Principle 1, entities must maintain transparency, and where adverse effects occur, greater care must be taken for transparent disclosures. Under Principle 3, entities are specifically obligated to prevent all forms of bonded/involuntary labour and ensure a workplace that is safe and free of harassment. Falsely reporting zero grievances directly compromises ethics and employee well-being.

questions.category: Integrated Scenario - BRSR Principles & ESG Assurance
questions.question:
CASE STUDY:
GreenHorizon Infrastructure Ltd., a top-500 listed infrastructure company, undertook the construction of a 200 km greenfield highway corridor. During the financial year 2023-24, the following issues arose:
1. The project displaced 600 tribal families from forest land. The company refused to pay rehabilitation compensation, claiming its 2% statutory CSR expenditure on urban digital schools exempts it from local resettlement obligations.
2. In its draft BRSR report, the company reported 100% compliance with human rights and zero employee grievances, despite 45 pending sexual harassment and bonded labour complaints before the Internal Complaints Committee (ICC).
3. The company disclosed that it adopted renewable solar power for highway toll plazas, which it classified under 'Governance (G) - Corporate Governance'.
4. The management approached CA. Ananya to issue an assurance report on its BRSR under SSAE 3000, requesting her to bypass on-site site visits and skip reviewing management responses to avoid delays.

With reference to Issue 3, how should CA. Ananya advise management regarding the correct classification of renewable solar energy under the three pillars of ESG?
options: Renewable energy is an 'Environment Opportunity' and must be classified under the Environment (E) pillar, not under the Governance (G) pillar.
Renewable energy is a 'Product Liability' metric and must be classified under the Social (S) pillar.
Renewable energy represents 'Corporate Behaviour' and is correctly classified under Governance (G).
Renewable energy does not fall under any ESG pillar and should be omitted from BRSR.
questions.explanation: The Environmental (E) pillar covers climate policies, energy use, waste, pollution, and natural resource conservation. Specifically, renewable energy is recognized as an 'Environment Opportunity' within the Environmental (E) pillar. In contrast, Governance (G) encompasses internal governance systems, ownership, accounting, business ethics, and tax transparency. Therefore, classifying renewable solar energy under Governance is an error that must be corrected to Environment (E).

questions.category: Integrated Scenario - BRSR Principles & ESG Assurance
questions.question:
CASE STUDY:
GreenHorizon Infrastructure Ltd., a top-500 listed infrastructure company, undertook the construction of a 200 km greenfield highway corridor. During the financial year 2023-24, the following issues arose:
1. The project displaced 600 tribal families from forest land. The company refused to pay rehabilitation compensation, claiming its 2% statutory CSR expenditure on urban digital schools exempts it from local resettlement obligations.
2. In its draft BRSR report, the company reported 100% compliance with human rights and zero employee grievances, despite 45 pending sexual harassment and bonded labour complaints before the Internal Complaints Committee (ICC).
3. The company disclosed that it adopted renewable solar power for highway toll plazas, which it classified under 'Governance (G) - Corporate Governance'.
4. The management approached CA. Ananya to issue an assurance report on its BRSR under SSAE 3000, requesting her to bypass on-site site visits and skip reviewing management responses to avoid delays.

With reference to Issue 4, how should CA. Ananya respond to management's request to omit on-site assessment and skip review of management responses?
options: CA. Ananya can accept the request because SSAE 3000 allows assurance providers to rely entirely on management representations without performing any verification procedures.

CA. Ananya must reject the request because the established methodology to provide assurance on BRSR requires on-site assessment/verification of the ESG report, submission of findings, and a thorough review of responses and clarifications on findings before preparing the assessment report.
CA. Ananya can bypass on-site visits provided management pays an expedited professional fee premium.
CA. Ananya can omit verification procedures only if the engagement is classified as a reasonable assurance engagement instead of limited assurance.
questions.explanation: Under the established methodology for providing assurance on BRSR and the requirements of SSAE 3000, the practitioner must execute rigorous verification procedures, including preliminary review of the report, on-site assessment/verification, submission of assessment findings, review of management responses/clarifications, and preparation of the assessment report prior to issuing the assessment statement. Agreeing to bypass on-site verification and skip reviewing responses violates mandatory assurance methodology and professional due care.

questions.category: Role of Auditor - Climate-Related Risks in Audit of FS
questions.question:
Given below are two statements labeled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R):

Assertion (A): The statutory auditor of a company must consider climate-related risks when developing an understanding of the entity and assessing risks of material misstatement in the audit of financial statements.

Reason (R): Climate-related risks and transitioning environmental laws can have direct accounting implications on asset impairment, provisions, useful lives of depreciable assets, and going concern assessments under the applicable financial reporting framework.

In the context of the above statements, which of the following is correct?
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct, and Reason (R) correctly explains Assertion (A). Although the statutory auditor's primary objective is obtaining reasonable assurance that the financial statements are free from material misstatement, developing an understanding of the entity requires considering climate-related risks. These risks directly translate into potential financial misstatements—such as premature asset write-offs, impairment of polluting plants, contingent environmental liabilities, and threats to going concern—which makes considering climate risks essential for the financial statement audit.

questions.category: BRSR - Section C Disclosures
questions.question:
Given below are two statements labeled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R):

Assertion (A): In Section C of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR), a reporting entity is legally obligated to report on all Essential Indicators, whereas reporting on Leadership Indicators remains optional.

Reason (R): Essential Indicators cover fundamental data regarding the core elements of the nine BRSR principles, whereas Leadership Indicators provide additional aspirational inputs, advanced programmes, and life cycle assessments.

In the context of the above statements, which of the following is correct?
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct, and (R) accurately explains (A). Section C of BRSR differentiates disclosures into Essential Indicators and Leadership Indicators. Essential Indicators are mandatory disclosures designed to capture baseline performance on core elements across all nine principles. Leadership Indicators are optional/aspirational disclosures intended for entities seeking to demonstrate higher sustainability maturity, such as life-cycle assessments and advanced supply-chain initiatives. Thus, (R) provides the exact regulatory rationale for why Essential Indicators are mandatory while Leadership Indicators are optional.
